analytic.title: Acquisition and Service of Temporal Data for Real-Time Plant Monitoring

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.head: Data sampled from plants are registered as temporal data, combined with time stamps. We developed a realtime data server which periodically acquires temporal data and transmits them to clients for graphic presentation. The real-time data server consists of multi threads scheduled based on the rate monotonic theory. This paper explains the design of a real-time data server.
div.p: The prediction for schedulability of it based on the rate monotonic theory has been verified with an experiment on an actual system.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: In plant monitoring, data must be acquired in a fixed period. Acquired data are combined with time stamps, and regarded as temporal data. The temporal data are important in the two meaning, i.e. maintenance and watching. The correctness of the time stamp is indispensable in the maintenance activities, because the order of the changes in the data is significant for identifying a fault. Sampling rate should be short enough because minute data conmbutes to the diagnosis. For plant operators who look out for a sudden disorder, however, it is important that they can understand what the data implies at a glance. Current sampled data should be periodically presented at rate appropriate for the operators to understand them. Past temporal data should be also retrieved during the data acquisition. When the operators scrutinize the plant, they want the temporal data in arbitrary periods to be retrieved. The most important point is that the data should be graphically displayed. The 'interleaving' between real-time acquisition of data and graphical presentation of the data to the plant operators is essential in plant monitoring systems. We have developed a real-time data server which periodically acquires temporal data and serves them to graphical software tools on UNIX.

It has been hard to design a real-time system because of difficulties in predicting the schedulability of the real-time system when it works actually. As a means to guarantee the schedulability of real-time systems, Liu and Layland have proposed the rate monotonic theory [6]. To apply it, however, all tasks in the real-time system have to be independent with each other. We design a real-time data server as an object which is composed of multi threads. With a new management method of temporal data, threads in the realtime data server can be regarded independent. The management method allows us to construct a real-time data server whose schedulability is predictable. The real-time data server interleaves the real time data acquisition and the interaction between the graphical software tools and itself.

The former part of this paper explains the design of a real-time data server. The prediction of the schedulability based on the rate monotonic theory has been verified with an experiment on an actual system. The detail of the experiment is illustrated in the latter part of this paper.

div.head: Significance
div.p: Though various methods are studied for the management of temporal data [3,7], they are not applicable in real-time systems. [8] which discusses a method for data handling in a real-time activity does not take the schedulability into consideration. A real-time data server is significant in the following two points.

The first point is distinction a hard real-time task from a soft real-time task. As described in [8], data acquisition is a hard real-time task, while graphic presentation of acquired data is a soft real-time task. We have developed a real-time data server which periodically acquires temporal data and serves them to graphical software tools on UNIX. Though it is impossible to guaranteed real time behaviors of programs on UNIX, frequent changes in layout in graphical presentation are preferred to the punctual presentation.

If the temporal data are transmitted to software tools on UNIX, plant monitoring systems are constructed at low cost, because the window systems are available on UNIX. They graphically present data to plant operators using library functions which are already developed for a window system. The correctness of time stamp in temporal data is necessary for diagnosis. When the operators scrutinize the plant, the temporal data must express the correct order of changes in the plant. The more minute the data are, the more easily the operators can identify a fault. Therefore, the real-time data server acquires temporal data in a strict periodic manner, while it serves the data to graphical software tools on UNIX.

The second point is a predictable design of a real-time data server. We assume that aperiodic tasks which have dead lines are not requested of a real-time data server. In plant monitoring, periodic task is dominant. Especially, data sampled from plant is valid only when they are acquired every specified period. Periodic data acquisition is a hard real-time task. Periodic behavior of a real-time data server is guaranteed based on the rate monotonic scheduling algorithm. The schedulability of a given periodic task set can be predicted, if each task in the set is independent with any other tasks[l,6,10]. Since the performance of a real-time data server can be estimated before it is built up, it can be developed without useless investment.

div.head: Temporal data
div.p: A set of variables whose values are process values can represent states of a plant. We refer to these variables as characteristic variables. A time point can be represented by a distance from a specific basis. A temporal datum is a set of characteristic variable values and a time stamp corresponding to the time point at which the values are sampled.
A series[ll] is a time-ordered set of temporal data whose time stamps increase in a monotonic rate[see fig. 11. We refer to a temporal datum in a series as a scene.

The temporal data are not always sampled in a certain rate. We assume that a temporal datum sampled in period [ b+n.c, b+(n+l).c ) can be regarded as a scene sampled at time point b+n c. We refer to constant c as the rate of the series. The rate determines the accuracy of the series in representing a state transition of a plant.

div.head: Multi thread object
div.p: A multi thread object [4] is proposed as a paradigm to construct a modularized real-time server. As shown in fig. 2, a multi thread object consists of more than one threads and a shared memory between them. It receives a request from a client, and executes methods to accomplish the request.

A server consisting of a single thread is not desirable for real-time applications because an arrival of a high priority request could not cause a high priority request arriving later to preempt calculation for a low priority request arriving earlier. A multi thread object solves the problem using two kinds of threads: a mother thread and child threads. The mother thread determines a method when a request arrives. It does not execute the method but entrusts the execution of the method to a child thread so that it may immediately check whether another request arrives. The child thread accomplishes the requested task by execution of the method. Each child thread is scheduled based on its priority. A thread which accomplishes a urgent request may finish earlier than a thread of a low priority, preempting the calculation which has already started.

div.head: Tasks in real-time data server
div.p: As shown in fig. 3, a real-time data server is connected with sensors on a real-time network. Process values sampled from a plant are periodically written on the memory within the real-time data server. The real-time data server forms temporal data[3, 71, attaching time stamps to the process values read from the memory. It always has to finish the attachment of a time stamp and the registration of each temporal datum within a cycle.

Software tools on UNIX computers are clients of a realtime data server. The clients may require the real-time data server the periodic transmission of the latest temporal datum. The real-time data server starts the periodic transmission. In addition to this kind of requests, the clients may aperiodically require to retrieve temporal data in a specific period. The real-time data server composes series of registered temporal data according to each request.
We refer to reading activated by the former request as periodic reading, while reading corresponding to the latter one as request driven reading.

All messages between clients and the real-time data server are transmitted based on UDP/IP protocol. When a client sends a message to start or to stop a periodic reading task, the real-time data server acknowledges the request. In case of starting a periodic reading task, a series consisting of the latest temporal datum is sent to the client every cycle specified in the request. The periodic reading is a soft realtime task whose deadline is the specified cycle. It is assumed that a request driven reading task has no deadline. When a client requests to perform it, the real-time data server sends a series consisting of temporal data in the specified period. Since it does not acknowledge the request, the client should prepare any means for fear the series should be lost for some reasons.

div.head: Realization using multi threads
div.p: A real-time data server is realized as a multi-thread object. Its components are shown in fig. 4. The acquisition thread periodically samples a new datum from a memory where data sampled from a plant are written, and forms a temporal datum by attaching a time stamp to the sampled datum. It registers the temporal datum on aring buffer. The saving thread periodically copies a part of temporal data on the ring buffer in a file on a disk, before the part is overwritten.

The receiver thread catches a message from a client and put it in the receiving queue. The mother thread gets the message to determine what method should be executes to accomplish a requested task specified in the message. The mother thread activates a child thread to executes the determined method. If the periodic reading is requested, a child thread is created to periodically transmit a series composed of the latest temporal datum. Methods for the request driven reading are executed in the lowest priority. The mother thread puts a message for request driven reading in the query queue. A child thread which works in background [5] starts to retrieve temporal data in a period specified in the message, after it gets out the message from the query queue. It converts the retrieved temporal data into a series which is an answer for the request.

All child threads put series in the transmitting queues. There are three transmitting queues; a queue to contain acknowledgements for requests to starthtop the periodic reading, a queue to contain series composed in periodic reading tasks, and a queue where threads for the request driven reading put series. To quickly send an acknowledgement, the first queue has the highest priority, while the last has the lowest one. The transmitter threads for each queue send responses to clients, blocking other transmitter threads during their transmission. After a transmitter thread finishes to send a message, it takes some time to get out another message. If only one transmitter thread were assigned to each transmitting queue, messages in a transmitting queue in higher priority cannot be sent continuously, but a message of lower priority would get the right to be transmitted. Therefore, two transmitter threads are prepared for each queue.

div.head: Two level ring structure:
div.p: A real-time data server has to retain temporal data sampled in a long term. Since temporal data on the ring buffer will be overwritten in hread Fig. 5 2 Level Ring Structure some time, they are copied to one of contiguous file@] which form a big ring structure, as shown in f i g 5 We refer to the ring structure as a ring file. Temporal data in the ring file are overwritten in a cycle which is far longer than that of the ring buffer.

Since a periodic reading thread has to send a series periodically, all temporal data necessary for the periodic reading should stay on the ring buffer for one cycle of the periodic reading. In the present design of the real-time data server, only the latest temporal datum is read from the ring buffer. The temporal datum necessary for the periodic reading is always on the ring buffer. In case that a series consisting of several temporal data is required in the periodic reading, the ring buffer is large enough for all temporal data retrieved in the periodic reading of the longest cycle to be stable on the ring buffer in the cycle.
On the contrary, a request driven reading has no deadline. It reads late temporal data from the ring buffer, and past temporal data from the ring file.

div.head: Optimistic reading:
div.p: Let us think of forming a se- ries of a specific rate and in a specific period. The series is composed of temporal data read from the two level ring structure. If no temporal datum were overwritten during the reading, all temporal data can be read without conflict from the two level ring structure. This is not the case in an actual system. The acquisition thread and the saving thread always overwrite some parts of the two level ring structure, preempting reading tasks. A temporal datum to be read might be inconsistent.

A periodic reading thread composes a series every cycle. The ring buffer is large enough to retain all temporal data necessary for the series during the cycle. Temporal data accessed by periodic reading threads are never overwritten during the cycle.

Since a request driven thread works in background, temporal data which it aims to read might be overwritten. A request driven reading thread performs optimistic reading: the optimistic reading assumes no temporal datum is overwritten. A thread to perform the optimistic reading has to check a result of the reading. For this purpose, the thread takes advantages of values of time stamps in temporal data. Since temporal data are acquired periodically, values of time stamps in the two level ring structure increase in a monotonic manner from the oldest temporal datum to the latest one. The thread read temporal data one by one according to a specific rate. It can identify a period which should include the time stamp of the next temporal datum to be read. When the thread reads a temporal datum from the two level ring structure, the time stamp of the temporal datum which is not included in an expected period means that the temporal datum is inconsistent because of the overwriting.

When the request driven reading thread which reads the ring buffer finds an inconsistent temporal datum, it compensates the result of the optimistic reading to keep c o n s i s t e n c y . For t h e c o n s i s t e n c y , we a s s u r e serializability [2] in the access of the ring buffer. The serializability prescribes that the acquisition thread should proceed any of the request driven reading threads. That is, when both the acquisition thread and the request driven reading thread access a same temporal datum on the ring buffer, the latter gets an overwritten temporal datum. In such a case, The request driven reading thread discards the overwritten one and gets a temporal datum in the same period from the ring file. When a temporal datum from a ring file turns out to be overwritten, the request driven reading thread cannot compensate the result of the optimistic reading.

div.head: Mutual exclusion: Since several threads access
div.p: the two level ring structure, each tread should exclude other threads during its access. However, a blocking time is too long if the access to the whole of the two level ring structure is prohibited in the exclusion. A lock by the request driven reading thread would prevent the acquisition thread from periodically registering the latest temporal datum. In a real-time data server, not the whole ring structure but a management tuple is locked when any thread accesses the two level ring structure. Moreover, the lock of the management tuple is implemented using a semaphore based on the priority inheritance protocol [9] to avoid the priority inversion.

Let I, the index of the oldest temporal datum on the ring buffer, and B, the time stamp of it. Similarly, let I, and Be the index of the latest temporal datum and the time stamp of it, respectively. Assume I, is the index of the oldest temporal datum which the saving thread does not copy to a contiguous file, and Fu is the index of the contiguous file the saving thread is updating. The management tuple of the two level ring structure is a set of I,,B,, Ie,BeI,, and F,.

The acquisition thread locks the management tuple for the duration of both registration of a new temporal datum on the ring buffer and update of the management tuple. The saving thread locks the management tuple during its update of F,, before it starts to copy temporal data to another contiguous file.

Threads accessing the ring buffer lock the management tuple only while they read the management tuple so that they might not block other threads of high priority for a long time. The periodic reading threads compose series of temporal data the acquisition thread has just registered on the ring buffer. It locks the management tuple during the reference of Ie and Be, before it reads the ring buffer. The request driven reading thread refers the values in the management tuple only once just after it gets a request message from the query queue. It calculates the indexes of temporal data to be read based on the referred values. Since the request driven reading thread works in background, temporal data to be read may be overwritten. Therefore, the request driven reading thread performs an optimistic reading of the temporal data.

The management tuple is small enough. The priority inheritance protocol assures that a thread accessing the management tuple blocks other threads for a minimum time. This assurance enables to neglect a blocking time necessary for the mutual exclusion of the management tuple. Therefore, the each thread of a real-time data server can be regarded as independent. The rate monotonic theory can be applied to guarantee that the threads should behave periodically.

div.head: Evaluation
div.p: We refer to the number of characteristic variables of a temporal datum on the ring buffer as the sampling size, and the cycle in which the acquisition thread registers a temporal datum on the ring buffer as the sampling rate. Let us think of schedulability of a real-time data server under various combinations of the sampling size, the sampling rate, and the number of periodic reading threads. We first predict the minimum sampling rate under which the real-time data server is schedulable for the given sampling size and the given number of the periodic reading threads. The prediction is verified with an experiment on an actual realtime data server.

div.head: Implementation
div.p: A real-time data server is constructed on real-time operating system Lynx386 which has facilities based on POSIX 1003.4. In this implementation, process values are not sampled from a plant, but an emulator thread generates process values in the same cycle as the acquisition thread so that the sampling size might be modified easily.

Each characteristic variable is @bit in data length. Each periodic reading thread forms a series which has one scene consisting of three characteristic variables every second. We created the periodic reading threads one by one to know when the real-time data server is not schedulable.

The load of periodic reading threads is so small that the main memory overflows before the real-time data server reaches its limit in the schedulability. Therefore, we add extra load to the periodic reading thread by looping. The CPU time spent for one cycle of the periodic reading is 11.2msec without the extra load and 161.2msec with the extra load.

div.head: Prediction and verification
div.p: In this experiment, the five kinds of threads are working; the acquisition thread, the saving thread, the periodic reading threads, the transmitter threads of medium priority, and the emulator thread. Since any other transmitter thread does not work, the two transmitter threads of medium priority are not blocked because of other transmitter threads. Therefore, threads in a real-time data server are blocked only when they access the two level ring structure. We regard the blocking time is small enough to be neglected.

Suppose that there are m periodic reading threads. When the following enequation is satisfied, a set of threads in the real-time data server is schedulable [6]. The left side of the enequation corresponds to the utilization [6]. When m=3, the value of the right side of the enequation is 72.86%. Let r the sampling rate. The values of the left side are 84.11% and 66.25% when r=lOmsec and r=20msec, respectively. The sampling rate which guarantees the schedulability of the real-time data server is 20msec.

Similarly, the sampling rate which guarantees the schedulability is calculated, letting the sampling size 31, 63, 127, 191, 255, 319, 383, 447, and 511. The calculation is done for two cases of the number of the periodic reading threads; 3 threads and 4 threads. The dotted line in fig. 6 shows the result of the calculation. The results presents the prediction of the sampling rate in which the actual real-time data server will be schedulable. Since the enequation represents a very pessimistic condition to guarantee the schedulability[lO], an actual real-time data server is considered to be schedulable even in a shorter sampling rate than the predicted one.

div.head: Fig.6 Prediction with RM and Result of Experiment
div.p: The minimum sampling rate in which the actual realtime data server is schedulable is presented by solid lines in fig. 6. Fig. 6 shows that the actual real-time data server is schedulable in the sampling rate which is shorter than the predicted one. This verification makes it clear that a realtime data server can be designed with predictability, if the CPU time of each thread is known.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: This paper explains the design of a real-time data server which periodically acquires temporal data from plant and serves them to software tools according to their requests. A real-time data server is constructed as a multi thread object. The schedulability of a real-time data server can be predictable, because the blocking time of threads is small enough to be neglected. The prediction of schedulability is verified with an experiment on an actual system. We assume that aperiodic tasks which have dead lines are not requested of a real-time data server. A sporadic serverll21 is necessary to guarantee of accomplishment of such tasks within a dead line. We also assume a real-time data server acquires temporal data periodically. We have to develop a systematic method to manage periodic temporal data and temporal data which are sampled on specific events. They are our future works.
